nameStory: The wild potato vine gets its name from its enormous underground tubers that can weigh up to 30 pounds! These massive root vegetables look like giant sweet potatoes and were historically roasted and eaten by Native Americans. The alternate name "man of the earth" refers to these impressive underground tubers that seem almost human-sized lurking beneath the soil.
description: Wild potato vine is a twining perennial vine that scrambles over bushes and fences with heart-shaped leaves and beautiful white morning-glory flowers. The vine can climb 10-15 feet high, wrapping around anything it can reach with its flexible stems. What makes this plant truly unique is hidden underground - massive potato-like tubers that can grow enormous over many years. It's extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation in the region.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large white funnel-shaped flowers about 3 inches across with a soft pinkish blush deep in the throat, opening in morning like other morning-glories and feeling papery-smooth to touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves that feel slightly fuzzy underneath and can vary from simple hearts to having subtle side lobes that give them a fiddle-like outline

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Vigorous twining vine that spirals clockwise around supports, with stems that feel smooth and flexible when young but become somewhat woody with age

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Massive underground tubers that can be several feet long and weigh many pounds - these giant "wild potatoes" are the plant's trademark feature though rarely seen

habitat: Found along woodland edges, fence rows, and disturbed areas with rich, deep soil that can accommodate its massive root system. Prefers partial sun to light shade and well-drained but moist soils. In New England, this southern species reaches the very northern edge of its range and is extremely uncommon.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the large underground tuber, sending up flexible green vines that begin climbing nearby supports.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with showy white morning-glory flowers opening in early morning hours, followed by small round seed capsules.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow before frost kills back the above-ground portions, while the massive tuber remains safely underground.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant above ground with all growth dying back to the large perennial root system below the frost line.

funFact: The underground tubers of wild potato vine can live for decades and grow to enormous sizes - some have been documented weighing over 30 pounds, making them among the largest plant roots in North America!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with common morning-glory, but wild potato vine has distinctly white flowers (not purple or blue) with a pinkish throat, and much more robust, woody stems. The heart-shaped leaves are also typically larger and fuzzier underneath than common morning-glory.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name "wild potato," this plant is actually more closely related to sweet potatoes than regular potatoes. The roots are edible when cooked but can cause digestive upset when raw, so they should never be eaten without proper preparation.
compareHints: Among New England morning-glories, wild potato vine stands out with its pure white flowers that have pink throats, while most others have purple, blue, or pink flowers. It's also much more robust and woody than relatives like common morning-glory or ivy-leaved morning-glory, with notably larger, fuzzier heart-shaped leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common morning-glory has the largest flowers among New England's morning-glories, with those distinctive heart-shaped leaves that lack the three-lobed structure of ivy-leaved morning-glory.

Among New England morning-glories, ivy-leaved is distinguished by its three-lobed leaves - common morning-glory has unlobed heart-shaped leaves, while white morning-glory has much smaller flowers and often heart-shaped but sometimes three-lobed leaves.

Garden Morning Glory stands out from its Ipomoea cousins with its large flower size and vibrant blue color range - Common Morning Glory has smaller, more purple-pink flowers, while Ivy-leaved Morning Glory has distinctly lobed leaves rather than the simple heart shape.
Cypress vine is instantly distinguished from all other morning glories by its incredibly fine, thread-like leaf segments - every other morning glory in New England has broad, solid leaves.

Among its morning glory relatives, moonflower stands out for its exclusively nighttime blooming and pure white color - most other Ipomoea species bloom during the day in shades of purple, blue, pink, or red.
Unlike its morning glory relatives that are primarily grown for their showy trumpet flowers, sweet potato is grown for foliage and edible tubers, rarely flowering in New England's climate.
Red morning glory stands out from other New England morning glories primarily by its small size and brilliant red color - most others have much larger purple, blue, or white flowers.

Among New England morning glories, scarlet creeper is the only one with consistently bright red flowers - common morning glory has purple flowers, ivy-leaved morning glory has blue to purple blooms, and moonflower has large white flowers.

White morning-glory stands out from its Ipomoea relatives by having the smallest flowers in the genus - much tinier than the dinner-plate-sized blooms of moonflower or the vibrant purple trumpets of common morning-glory.
